questions.prompt: DESIGN IT — [senior] correcting issued invoices: credit notes, refunds, tax rounding and legal numbering (organized-study-enterprise-billing-platform, docs/system-design-current.md). Scenario: a year after launch the platform takes on its first European tenants, 1,200 of them billing in euros with VAT shown per invoice line; support now handles about 400 corrections a month (wrong seat counts, goodwill credits, duplicate charges to give back); a tenant in Los Angeles complains that invoices meant for the 1st are dated the last day of the previous month; and the finance team must hand auditors invoice numbers with no gaps and no reuse. Write your design before you look: what happens to an invoice that is wrong after it was issued, and how that differs once it has been paid; how giving money back relates to the payment and to the invoice; where tax is rounded when an invoice has several lines; how 'the 1st' is decided for each tenant; how legal numbers are allocated for invoices and corrections; and what each correction leaves behind for audit and for downstream systems. Then tick the checkpoints you covered and add up the weights (suggested pass: 70% with every [w3] hit)

keyPoints.text: [w3] An issued invoice is never edited: the declared moves let an open invoice be voided, but a paid one has no way out at all, so a correction after issue is a separate credit note that references the original, carries its own lines and amounts, and leaves the first document standing as evidence; the schema has no such document yet, only invoices and their lines.

[w3] Giving money back is a refund of a payment, not a change to the invoice: today a payment's status ends at succeeded or failed, with no refunded amount and no refund record, so the design adds refunds that point at a payment, are capped by what that payment captured minus what was already returned, and are tracked apart from any credit note, because either can exist without the other.

[w3] VAT per line needs tax stored per line: an invoice line today keeps a description, quantity, unit amount and subtotal but no rate and no tax amount, so the design records each line's rate and rounded tax and states the rounding rule on the invoice. The rule matters: three 333-cent lines at 20% give 67 cents each, 201 in total, while taxing the 999-cent sum gives 200.

[w3] 'The 1st' belongs to the tenant: an organization carries no time zone, and periods are computed from the server's current instant, so a run at midnight UTC is still the previous afternoon in Los Angeles; the design stores a billing time zone per tenant, turns local midnight into a UTC instant when a period is created, and writes that boundary onto the invoice.

[w3] Legal numbers are allocated at issue, per series: today a number is assigned the moment an invoice row is created, and every invoice is created already open and finalized, so a future draft stage would burn numbers on documents that never go out. Numbers are taken only when a document is issued, a void keeps its number and its row, and credit notes run in a series of their own.

[w2] Prorated corrections round in exactly one place: money refuses anything but whole cents, so a seat-count fix for part of a period is computed as a fraction of the line, rounded once by a stated rule, and the rounding difference is written down instead of being absorbed somewhere else.

[w2] A correction stays in its invoice's currency: adding amounts in two currencies throws, so a credit note or refund for a euro invoice is issued in euros, and an exchange-rate change is never treated as a correction.

[w1] Every correction writes an audit row with actor and reason and an outbox event in the same transaction, the way the existing commands already do, so the ledger, the customer email and any accounting export learn about it without a second write path.
keyPoints.quote: Audit logs and outbox events from the beginning.

questions.prompt: PRE-MORTEM — the correction features have been live for a quarter. A support agent 'fixes' a paid invoice by flipping it to void in the database and issuing a new one; a refund call to the payment provider times out and the agent presses refund again; the Los Angeles tenant's October revenue report is missing the invoices for its 1 November renewals; a customer's accountant adds up the per-line VAT and lands one cent away from the invoice's tax; and a full credit note issued against a 665-cent line taxed at 10% leaves the customer owing one cent. What breaks, how does each show up, and what in your design prevents it?

keyPoints.text: [w3] Status edits outside the transition rules are the root of the void-a-paid-invoice fix: nothing in the running code consults the declared moves, so any writer can set any status, and a voided paid invoice leaves a successful payment pointing at a dead document. Route every status change through one correction service that applies the transition table, and make a paid invoice correctable only by issuing a credit note.

[w3] The second refund press is a second refund unless the first attempt has an identity: today the provider reference on a payment is minted from the clock at each attempt, so nothing stable ties a retry to the first try. Create the refund row before calling the provider, pass its id as the provider's idempotency key, and let a retry reuse that row and key instead of making another.

[w3] The renewals were created at midnight UTC, which is still the afternoon of 31 October in Los Angeles, so any report that buckets by creation time lands them in the wrong month for that tenant. Store the billed period on the invoice and report revenue by that period in the tenant's zone, never by the instant the row was written.

[w2] The one-cent VAT gap is a rounding-rule mismatch: the calculator produces one tax amount for the whole invoice while the accountant sums rounded line amounts, so with per-line VAT the invoice's tax must be the sum of the rounded line taxes, and the rule printed on the document must be the one its totals obey.

[w3] A credit note built by negating the amounts and re-running the same arithmetic does not net to zero at half-cents: tax is rounded with Math.round, which sends halves toward positive infinity, so 10% of 665 cents rounds to 67 while 10% of minus 665 rounds to minus 66, leaving one cent owed. Take a credit's tax from the original line's stored tax, or round symmetrically away from zero.

[w1] Reconcile money and documents daily per tenant: invoices minus credit notes must equal payments minus refunds plus what is still open, and any tenant whose two sides disagree goes to a review list before month end.

questions.prompt: TRADE-OFF HANDBACK — defend your correction design against the alternatives: voiding and reissuing versus issuing credit notes; rounding tax per line versus once per invoice; billing on each tenant's local calendar versus one UTC calendar for everyone; a counter row versus a database sequence versus allocating at issue for legal numbers; and refunding to the card versus leaving an account credit. For each, say what you bought and what it cost.

keyPoints.text: [w3] Void and reissue gives the customer one clean document and suits an open invoice nobody has paid, which the declared moves already allow; once paid, or once a jurisdiction forbids altering issued documents, a credit note is the only honest path, at the cost of two documents the customer must read together and reports that net them.

[w3] Per-line rounding matches what customers' accounting and many VAT rules expect and makes every line self-explanatory, at the cost of totals a few cents away from whole-invoice arithmetic; rounding once is closest to the exact amount, but its line amounts no longer add up. Either way the rule is a stored property of the invoice, chosen per jurisdiction, just as tax rates themselves must stop being one setting per tenant.

[w2] Local calendars bill each tenant at its own midnight, which also spreads the 1st-of-month peak across the world's time zones; one UTC calendar is a single batch at a single instant and simpler to test, at the cost of dates that look wrong to everyone far from UTC. Either is new work, since a subscription period is only a count of days today; local calendars also cost a stored zone per tenant and boundaries that respect daylight saving.

[w2] A counter row incremented in the issuing transaction rolls back with it, so it never skips a number, but every issue for that tenant waits on that row; a database sequence never waits, yet a rolled-back transaction leaves a hole a legal series cannot have; allocating only at issue keeps drafts from consuming numbers whichever mechanism hands them out.

[w2] A card refund returns real money and settles the complaint, at the cost of provider fees, refund windows and a second money movement to track; an account credit keeps the cash and applies to the next invoice, but needs a credit balance per customer that the schema does not have and a rule for paying out a customer who leaves.
[w1] Prove the correction path against a real provider's refund semantics before relying on it, since the mock provider here decides success by arithmetic and has no refund call at all.
keyPoints.quote: Mock provider before real Stripe integration to make workflow behavior inspectable.
